connection: Session 21 covered dependency injection. This session reads the real PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours line by line: a Where-shaped filter inside GetEmployeeClockEntries, feeding a Sum with an inline projection -- one LINQ pipeline split across two real methods.
objectives: Read GetEmployeeClockEntries as a Where pipeline: employeeId match, ClockOut not null, and a date range, all in one lambda.
Read CalculateTotalHours's .Sum(x => x.GetDuartion().TotalHours) as a projection and aggregation combined into a single call, not a separate Select stage.
Explain decision-0007: why the real code chose one combined LINQ call over three separate named pipeline stages.
Write a new query using the same Where-then-Sum-with-projection shape against ClockEntryQueries.cs.

visuals.title: GetEmployeeClockEntries filters, in one compound Where
visuals.explanation: entry.EmployeeId == employeeId && entry.ClockOut != null && entry.ClockIn >= startDate && entry.ClockIn <= endDate -- three real AND-ed conditions in one lambda.

visuals.title: CalculateTotalHours projects and aggregates in one Sum call
visuals.explanation: .Sum(x => x.GetDuartion().TotalHours) -- decision-0007: no separate Select stage exists in the real code.

visuals.title: TotalHours, not Hours
visuals.explanation: TimeSpan.Hours truncates to a 0-23 component; TotalHours is the real, full duration CalculateTotalHours actually sums.

visuals.explanation: Two mocked shifts of 2 and 3 hours sum to exactly 5.0 through the real GetEmployeeClockEntries + CalculateTotalHours pipeline.

preQuiz.prompt: In the real GetEmployeeClockEntries, what does the .Where() lambda filter on?
options: employeeId match, ClockOut not null, and ClockIn within the given date range -- all three conditions in one lambda
preQuiz.explanation: The real method combines three AND-ed conditions in a single Where call, confirmed against Repositories/ClockEntryRepository.cs.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does CalculateTotalHours use .Sum(x => x.GetDuartion().TotalHours) instead of a separate .Select(...).Sum() pipeline?
options: Both forms are valid LINQ; the real code chose the inline one-liner and never had a separate Select stage or GetCompletedDurations method (decision-0007)
C# does not allow chaining Select before Sum
GetDuartion cannot be called inside a Select
preQuiz.explanation: decision-0007 documents that the originally planned three-stage pipeline was never built -- the real code combines projection and aggregation in one Sum call.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does TotalHours matter more than Hours in this Sum call?
options: TimeSpan.Hours truncates to whole hours within a day, so a 26-hour shift would report 2, not 26; TotalHours reports the true total
TotalHours is required syntax for Sum
Hours and TotalHours are identical for this domain
preQuiz.explanation: TimeSpan.Hours is the hours component (0-23) of the span, not the full duration -- using it here would silently corrupt payroll totals for any shift over 24 hours.

concept.title: Where filters with a compound condition
paragraphs: GetEmployeeClockEntries filters _clockEntries with one Where call carrying three AND-ed conditions: the right employee, a completed entry, and inside the date range.
Reading it left to right: entries -> keep matching employeeId -> keep completed -> keep in range. No loop, no accumulator variable -- the pipeline is the whole method body.

concept.title: Sum can project and aggregate in one call
paragraphs: CalculateTotalHours does not call .Select() at all. The lambda passed to .Sum() -- x => x.GetDuartion().TotalHours -- both transforms each ClockEntry into a number of hours AND feeds it straight into the running total.

This is decision-0007 in the source project's decision log: the original plan was three separate methods (GetCompletedEntries, GetCompletedDurations, then Sum); the delivered code is two methods, with projection folded into the aggregation.

concept.title: Verify with the real, existing test
paragraphs: PayrollServiceTests.cs already proves this pipeline: two mocked shifts of 2 and 3 hours sum to exactly 5.0 through GetEmployeeClockEntries and CalculateTotalHours together.

This session's lab writes a second, independent query (ClockEntryQueries.LongestFirst) using the same Where-then-project-and-aggregate shape, but ordered and filtered by a minimum-hours threshold instead.

postQuiz.prompt: If you needed the list of raw hour values before summing them (for a histogram, say), what would you add to CalculateTotalHours's pipeline?
options: A .Select(x => x.GetDuartion().TotalHours) stage before .Sum(), separating projection from aggregation
Nothing -- Sum already exposes the intermediate values
A foreach loop, since LINQ cannot expose intermediate values
postQuiz.explanation: This is exactly the three-stage pipeline decision-0007 says was originally planned but not needed for the single CalculateTotalHours caller -- it becomes worth adding once a second caller needs the intermediate values.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does GetEmployeeClockEntries filter on ClockOut != null?
options: An open (still-clocked-in) entry has no valid duration -- GetDuartion would throw if summed before completion
ClockOut is required by the LINQ Where method's signature
It has no effect; every entry always has ClockOut set
postQuiz.explanation: GetDuartion throws InvalidOperationException on an open entry; filtering ClockOut != null before the Sum call is what prevents that exception during payroll calculation.

postQuiz.prompt: What would happen if GetEmployeeClockEntries's Where predicate dropped the date-range conditions?
options: CalculateTotalHours would sum every completed shift the employee ever worked, not just the requested period
The method would fail to compile
Nothing -- the date parameters are unused
postQuiz.explanation: The date-range conditions are real, load-bearing parts of the compound Where -- removing them silently changes what CalculateTotalHours reports.

reflections: Why is a compound Where condition (three ANDs in one lambda) easier to reason about here than three separate filtering methods?
What would ClockEntryQueries.LongestFirst look like if it needed the intermediate hour values for something other than filtering?
Where else in this codebase could a Select-then-Sum split make a future second caller's job easier?
whatBreaks: Removing the ClockOut != null condition from GetEmployeeClockEntries reintroduces GetDuartion's InvalidOperationException into CalculateTotalHours. Removing the date-range conditions makes CalculateTotalHours silently ignore its own startDate/endDate parameters. Splitting Sum's inline projection into a separate Select adds an intermediate allocation with no current caller that needs it -- a real but currently unnecessary refactor.
summary: The real PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours is one Where-shaped filter (in GetEmployeeClockEntries) feeding one Sum call with an inline projection -- decision-0007 documents that this two-method, no-separate-Select shape was the delivered design, not the three-stage pipeline originally planned.
